section_title: What does the soldiers’ mock coronation reveal?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 16 Then the soldiers led Jesus away into the palace (that is, the Praetorium) and called the whole company together. 17 They dressed Him in a purple robe, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head. 18 And they began to salute Him: “Hail, King of the Jews!” 19 They kept striking His head with a staff and spitting on Him. And they knelt down and bowed before Him. 20 After they had mocked Him, they removed the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him out to crucify Him.
21 Now Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was passing by on his way in from the country, and the soldiers forced him to carry the cross of Jesus.

context_lines: The soldiers bring Jesus inside the palace and turn His kingship into a cruel performance. They put a purple robe and a crown of thorns on Him, salute Him as king, bow before Him, strike Him, and spit on Him. The gestures that imitate honor accompany real abuse.

When the mockery ends, they put His own clothes back on Him and lead Him away to crucifixion. They compel a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, to carry His cross. Mark names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus, but does not tell us when they came to faith or identify Rufus with the man later greeted in Romans. ([Romans 16:13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/16.htm))

John records Jesus setting out carrying His cross, while Luke describes Simon carrying it behind Him. The accounts give us those details without recording the familiar later picture of Jesus falling three times or telling us the exact point at which Simon was brought in. ([John 19:17](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/19.htm); [Luke 23:26](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/23.htm))
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readers commonly understand the robe, crown, greeting, and bowing as mock royal honors directed at Jesus. The Catholic study notes on the parallel scene explain the royal parody, while Mark’s wider story presents the king being mocked as the One whose authority will be revealed. ([USCCB, notes on Matthew 27:28–30](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/matthew/27); [Mark 14:62](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/14.htm))
god_plan_lines: Hebrews describes Jesus as crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, and connects that suffering with bringing God’s children to glory. The contrast with the soldiers’ crown is a useful parallel: human mockery does not determine the honor God gives His Son. His suffering serves the salvation of others. ([Hebrews 2:9–13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/2.htm))

The same passage explains that He shared human flesh and blood to break death’s power and free those enslaved by fear of death. He becomes a merciful high priest able to help the tempted. The abuse on this road belongs within that saving mission, and His people receive both help and an example of faithfulness in suffering. ([Hebrews 2:14–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/2.htm); [1 Peter 2:21–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/2.htm))
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
